lessons.title: User Groups & Who Participates in Sport
lessons.description: The twelve user groups and how their needs shape participation in sport.
lessons.content_html:
Who Takes Part in Sport?

Sport is for everyone — but not everyone experiences it in the same way. When sports organisations, councils and coaches plan activities, they need to think carefully about user groups: the distinct categories of people whose lives, responsibilities and backgrounds shape when, where and how they take part. Understanding user groups is the starting point for making sport genuinely inclusive.

Key Fact

There are twelve recognised user groups: gender, ethnic minorities, retired people and people over 60, families with children, carers, young children, teenagers, people with disabilities, single parents, people who work full-time, unemployed people, and people who are economically disadvantaged.

Gender

Men and women have historically participated in sport at different rates. While overall participation has become more balanced, gender still influences what sports are on offer, how much media coverage athletes receive, and whether someone feels welcome at a club. Sport England’s Active Lives survey consistently shows that women are less likely than men to meet physical activity guidelines. Initiatives such as the “This Girl Can” campaign have aimed to close this gap by challenging stereotypes around female participation.

Ethnic Minorities

People from ethnic minorities may face specific barriers to participation, including cultural expectations, language differences, a lack of visible role models, and sometimes discrimination. Sport has powerful potential to unite communities across ethnic lines, but that potential is only realised when clubs actively welcome all backgrounds. The proportion of Black, Asian and mixed-heritage athletes in elite sport varies enormously across disciplines.

Retired people and people over 60 may have more free time than working adults, but physical limitations, health conditions, or a lack of confidence can reduce participation. Sport for this group tends to focus on low-impact activities — walking football, swimming, bowls, and gentle yoga have all grown rapidly. Keeping older adults active reduces NHS costs and maintains independence. Walking football, for example, is now played in hundreds of clubs across the UK, giving retired people a social and physical outlet.

Families with Children

Families with children often struggle to find sports that all family members can enjoy together and that fit around school, childcare and work schedules. Cost is a major factor: kit, club fees and travel add up quickly when a family has two or three children. Facilities that offer family memberships or free junior sessions can make a significant difference. Many leisure centres now offer family swimming sessions or junior athletics days specifically to target this group.

Carers

A carer is someone who looks after a family member or friend who has a disability, illness or mental health condition. Carers often have very little time for themselves, and sport and physical activity may feel like a luxury they cannot afford. Targeted programmes — such as respite sports sessions where the person being cared for is also looked after — can open up participation for this group. Carers’ wellbeing is recognised as a public health priority, and regular physical activity significantly reduces carer burnout.

Young children (typically under 12) need sport and physical activity that is fun, safe and age-appropriate. Fundamental movement skills — running, jumping, throwing — are developed in these early years, and positive early experiences strongly predict adult participation. Schools and community clubs play the largest role here.

Teenagers face different challenges: peer pressure, self-consciousness, competing priorities such as exams and social media, and the transition from school sport to community clubs at age 16. Active Lives data shows participation drops sharply among 14-to-16-year-olds, particularly girls. Youth sport programmes that prioritise social connection alongside activity tend to retain teenagers better.

People with Disabilities

People with disabilities may have physical, sensory or cognitive impairments that affect how they can take part. Provision ranges from adapted mainstream sport — such as wheelchair basketball or blind cricket — to disability-specific events. Despite the inspiration of Paralympic athletes at Paris 2024, participation at grassroots level remains much lower than for non-disabled people. Physical access to facilities, specialist coaching and adapted equipment are all critical factors.

Key Fact

Sport England data consistently shows the lowest participation rates among people with disabilities, people from lower socio-economic backgrounds, and some ethnic minority groups. Addressing these gaps is a central aim of national sport strategy.

Single Parents and People Who Work Full-Time

Single parents carry childcare, domestic and financial responsibilities alone — meaning time and money for sport are in very short supply. Even a one-hour swimming lesson for a child requires arranging childcare for any other children. People who work full-time, particularly those doing shift work or long commutes, may only have early mornings or late evenings free. Gyms and leisure centres that open at 6 am or offer 45-minute lunchtime classes help reach this group.

Unemployed People and the Economically Disadvantaged

Economically disadvantaged individuals face direct cost barriers: club fees, kit, transport and facility entry fees. Unemployed people may have more time available but limited money. Concessionary pricing, free community sport schemes and lottery-funded programmes all attempt to widen access. The government’s “Holiday Activities and Food” programme is one example of using sport provision to reach low-income families during school holidays.

In exam answers, always use the precise user group names. Writing “old people” instead of “retired people / people over 60”, or “disabled” instead of “people with disabilities”, will lose marks because examiners credit only the specification wording. Similarly, “poor people” should be “economically disadvantaged” or “unemployed people” depending on which barrier you are describing. Precision matters — this is a closed list, not a general discussion.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When a question asks you to ‘identify’ a user group, use the exact words from the specification. ‘Old people’, ‘disabled’ or ‘poor people’ will not be credited — the correct terms are ‘retired people / people over 60’, ‘people with disabilities’ and ‘economically disadvantaged’. For ‘explain’ questions, always follow your identification with a reason: say why that group participates less, or what specifically affects their access to sport — not just who they are.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • There are twelve named user groups — including gender, ethnic minorities, retired people, carers, people with disabilities, single parents and the economically disadvantaged — each with distinct needs that affect how they participate in sport.
  • Examiners credit only the exact specification wording for user groups; informal labels like ‘old people’ or ‘disabled’ will lose marks.
  • Understanding each group’s characteristics is the foundation for identifying barriers and solutions — a chain that runs through all the participation topics that follow.

Example (up to 2 marks): for example, a family may not be able to afford a gym membership or the cost of a child's football kit and registration fee, meaning the child cannot join a local club (2 marks for a specific, applied example; 1 mark for a vague example). [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
Riverside Leisure Centre is redesigning its programme to attract more retired people and people over 60. At the moment, only 8% of its members are from this user group.

Discuss the factors a leisure centre manager should consider when trying to increase participation among retired people and people over 60.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): A balanced discussion covering at least two relevant factors from both sides or two perspectives, with specific examples applied to the scenario. For example: the need for low-impact, age-appropriate activities such as aqua aerobics or walking netball alongside the importance of social atmosphere; contrasted with the challenge that health conditions or lack of confidence may prevent this group from attending even well-designed sessions. Both factors are developed with reasoning.
Secure (3–4 marks): At least two relevant factors identified and briefly explained with some reference to the scenario context.
Developing (2 marks): One or two factors identified but not clearly explained or applied to the scenario.
Emerging (1 mark): A single relevant point with no development. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Springvale Sports Club has noticed that carers in the local area rarely use their facilities. The club wants to develop a targeted programme to increase participation among this user group.

Evaluate the extent to which understanding the specific needs of carers can help a sports club increase participation rates among this user group.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8 marks): A balanced evaluation that identifies carers’ specific needs (very limited time, financial pressure, difficulty leaving the person they care for), argues that understanding these needs allows the club to design appropriate solutions (respite sessions, flexible timetabling, subsidised fees), and then challenges this with the counter-argument that even perfectly targeted provision may not overcome the most fundamental barrier (the carer may simply be unable to leave the dependent individual). A clear, substantiated judgement is reached that goes beyond listing points.
Secure (5–6 marks): At least two relevant points on each side (or two well-developed points and one on the other side), with some application to the scenario and an attempt at a judgement.
Developing (3–4 marks): Relevant points identified but largely one-sided or without a clear judgement. Some reference to carers but limited specificity.
Emerging (1–2 marks): Basic points about carers or barriers with little development and no evaluation. [8 marks]

lessons.title: Barriers to Participation — and How to Remove Them
lessons.description: Nine barriers to sport participation, matched solutions, and how clubs remove them.
lessons.content_html:
Why Don’t People Participate?

Even when sport is on offer, many people never take part — or stop taking part. A barrier to participation is anything that gets in the way of someone being active. Understanding barriers is essential for sports clubs, leisure centres and national organisations because solving the wrong problem wastes resources. Identifying the right barrier for the right user group is the first step to removing it.

Key Fact

The nine barriers to participation are: employment and unemployment, family commitments, lack of disposable income, lack of transport, lack of role models, lack of activity provision, lack of awareness, media coverage (gender and ethnicity), and personal factors such as low self-esteem or perceived risk.

Employment and Unemployment

People in full-time employment often struggle to find time for sport around working hours, especially shift workers whose patterns change week to week. Unemployed people face the opposite problem — time may be available but money is scarce. For both groups, sport that is free or very low-cost and offered at flexible times is most likely to work. A solution for full-time workers might be a leisure centre that opens at 6 am and offers 45-minute express sessions.

Family Commitments

Parenting young children, caring for elderly relatives, or running a household all compete with time for sport. Single parents and carers are particularly affected because they often have no one to share these responsibilities with. Solutions include ‘buggy fitness’ classes where children attend alongside parents, family membership schemes, and on-site crèche provision at leisure centres. Creche availability is frequently cited by mothers as the single most important factor in their ability to exercise.

Disposable income is the money left over after essential bills are paid. Sport has many hidden costs beyond a club membership fee: kit, footwear, travel, match fees, specialist coaching and competition entry all add up. For economically disadvantaged families, these costs can put participation out of reach entirely. Solutions include concessionary pricing (discounted entry for those on benefits or low incomes), kit-swap schemes run by local authorities, and Sport England ‘Active Communities’ grants that fund free holiday sport programmes.

Lack of Transport

Sport facilities are not evenly distributed across the country. In rural areas, there may be no swimming pool, athletics track or sports hall within reasonable distance, and public transport links may be poor or non-existent. Even in cities, night-time training sessions can end after the last bus. Solutions include minibus schemes organised by clubs, locating new facilities on existing public transport corridors, and encouraging car-sharing among club members.

Lack of Role Models

Seeing someone who looks like you succeeding in a sport increases belief that participation is possible. The absence of visible role models from ethnic minority backgrounds, disability sport, or specific genders at elite level can make sport feel ‘not for people like me.’ Solutions include targeted media campaigns, athlete ambassador programmes, and ensuring representative coaches at grassroots level. The visibility of British wheelchair tennis players and blind footballers at Paris 2024 inspired thousands of young disabled people to enquire about their local clubs.

Some user groups — such as carers, retired people or people with certain disabilities — simply find that no suitable programme exists near them. A leisure centre that offers only five-a-side football and high-intensity circuits has not provided for these groups at all. Solution: sports clubs can create targeted programmes (walking netball, sitting volleyball, adapted badminton) specifically for underrepresented groups.

Even where provision exists, people may not know about it. Lack of awareness is particularly common among newer immigrant communities who are unfamiliar with local sport structures, and among older adults who may not use social media. Solutions include targeted promotion through community centres, GP referral schemes, leafleting in non-English languages, and word-of-mouth outreach through trusted community leaders.

Media Coverage: Gender and Ethnicity

The sports that receive the most media coverage attract the most participants. Women’s sport and disability sport have historically received far less broadcast time and newspaper coverage than men’s sport. This creates a cycle: less coverage means fewer visible role models, which means fewer women and disabled people try those sports, which means fewer compelling stories for broadcasters to cover. The growth in women’s football audiences — the Women’s Super League regularly drew over one million TV viewers per match in 2024-25 — shows how media investment can shift participation patterns.

Key Fact

Examiners reward barrier–solution pairings. The question will say ‘identify one barrier for [user group] and suggest one solution.’ A barrier without a matched solution, or a solution without a linked barrier, typically scores only half the available marks.

Solutions: Facility Access and Adapted Provision

Physical adapted provision is essential for people with disabilities. This includes wheelchair-accessible changing rooms and pool hoists for swimmers, hearing loops at reception and in fitness studios, braille signage for visually impaired users, and coaching qualifications that cover disability sport. A sports facility that lacks a pool hoist has effectively excluded all wheelchair users from aquatic activity, regardless of how welcoming the staff are.

Solutions: Pricing, Promotion and Taster Sessions

Concessionary pricing reduces cost barriers: councils and leisure trusts typically offer discounts to people on Universal Credit, Job Seekers’ Allowance, or disability benefits. Taster sessions — free, no-kit-required introductory classes — lower the psychological barrier of trying something unfamiliar. Targeted promotion means advertising where the target group already is: leaflets at food banks for economically disadvantaged families, posters in GP waiting rooms for retired people, and social media campaigns in minority languages for ethnic minority communities.

A very common error is to list several barriers and then separately list several solutions, without showing which solution addresses which barrier. The question typically asks you to identify a barrier and then suggest how to overcome it for a specific user group. The mark is awarded for the linkage — barrier X causes problem Y for group Z; solution A removes barrier X by doing B. Always write your answer as a chain, not two separate lists.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When a question asks you to ‘suggest a solution to a barrier’, make sure your solution directly addresses the barrier you named — not just any barrier. For example, if the barrier is ‘lack of transport’, a relevant solution is ‘a club minibus scheme’; saying ‘build more facilities’ would not directly remove the transport barrier and will not score. For ‘discuss’ questions, consider two or more user groups or two or more barriers — examiners reward answers that consider more than one viewpoint.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • There are nine barriers: employment/unemployment, family commitments, lack of disposable income, lack of transport, lack of role models, lack of activity provision, lack of awareness, and media coverage relating to gender and ethnicity.
  • Solutions must be matched to the specific barrier and user group — the linkage is what earns exam marks, not separate lists.
  • Adapted provision (hoists, hearing loops, braille signage), concessionary pricing, taster sessions and targeted promotion are the main solution categories to learn.

Solution with example (up to 2 marks): the club could organise a minibus to collect members from a central meeting point, funded by a community grant, which removes the transport cost and logistics barrier for unemployed people who may not be able to afford a car or taxi (2 marks for a clear, applied solution; 1 mark for a vague suggestion). practice_questions.text:
Ferndale Leisure Trust has identified that participation among single parents in their local area is very low. They have a limited budget.

Discuss the barriers single parents face when trying to participate in sport and how the leisure trust could overcome them.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): A developed discussion that names at least two specific barriers (e.g. family commitments, lack of disposable income, lack of suitable provision) and matches each to a realistic solution within a limited budget (e.g. crèche provision on-site, concessionary pricing, taster sessions at no cost, family swim sessions). Both barriers and solutions are clearly linked and the answer considers more than one perspective or challenge.

practice_questions.text:
Northgate Athletics Club has applied for a grant to improve participation among economically disadvantaged young people aged 11–16 in their town. The club is considering offering free taster sessions, subsidised kit loans, and a minibus from the town centre.

Evaluate how effective these three strategies are likely to be at removing the barriers faced by economically disadvantaged teenagers.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8 marks): A balanced evaluation that assesses all three strategies, explaining the specific barrier each targets (cost of trying, cost of kit, transport) and weighing effectiveness. The best answers argue that taster sessions remove the awareness and psychological barrier but not the ongoing cost barrier; subsidised kit loans address one major cost but not ongoing club fees; the minibus removes transport but only for those who know about the club and want to attend. A substantiated judgement is reached on which combination is most effective or what additional strategy would be needed.
Secure (5–6 marks): Two or more strategies evaluated with clear reasoning and some attempt at a judgement.
Developing (3–4 marks): Strategies described but evaluation is one-sided or judgement is missing.
Emerging (1–2 marks): Basic points about barriers or solutions with no evaluation. [8 marks]

lessons.title: Popularity of Sport in the UK & Emerging Sports
lessons.description: Eight factors shaping sport's popularity in the UK, plus how padel and pickleball are growing.
lessons.content_html:
Why Are Some Sports More Popular Than Others?

Sport does not become popular by accident. The sports millions of people play and watch — football, tennis, athletics — are popular because a combination of factors has come together over many decades. Understanding these factors helps explain why some sports thrive while others struggle to find participants, and why new sports can suddenly break through. There are eight key factors that drive the popularity of sport in the UK.

Key Fact

The eight factors affecting the popularity of sport are: number of people participating, provision of facilities, environment and climate, live spectator opportunities, media coverage and range, high-level success of national teams or athletes, positive role models, and social acceptability.

Participation Numbers and Facilities

Sports with large numbers of participants generate income through club fees, kit sales and lottery funding — which in turn funds more facilities, coaching and development. It is a positive cycle: the more people play, the better the infrastructure becomes, which attracts even more players. Football has over 11 million registered adult participants in England, making it by far the most played team sport and explaining why there are far more grass pitches per square kilometre than tennis courts.

Provision of facilities is closely linked to participation. If there is no swimming pool within 10 miles, swimming participation will be low in that area regardless of other factors. The closure of public swimming pools in the 2010s led to measurable drops in adult swimming participation in those communities.

Environment and Climate

The UK’s mild, wet climate favours some sports and hinders others. Outdoor cricket requires dry summers; the British weather limits the playing season and discourages casual participation. Winter sports such as skiing need consistent snowfall — which is why the UK produces far fewer elite skiers than alpine nations. Conversely, the UK’s coastline and tidal rivers support a healthy sailing and rowing culture. Climate is not destiny, but it shapes which sports are practical to participate in without expensive facilities.

Being able to watch sport live — at a stadium, an athletics track, or a community pitch — creates emotional attachment and interest that drives participation. A child who attends a Premier League match is more likely to join a local football club than a child who has only watched from home. Premier League stadia regularly sell out at 50,000-plus capacity; the spectator culture this creates sustains grassroots interest.

Media coverage is perhaps the most powerful driver of popularity in the modern era. A sport broadcast on free-to-air television reaches tens of millions of viewers; one locked behind a subscription paywall reaches far fewer. The BBC’s coverage of Wimbledon annually peaks at around 9 million viewers and produces a documented spike in junior tennis sign-ups. The range of sports covered matters too: if a sport appears only once every four years (e.g. at the Olympics), it struggles to build sustained public awareness compared with a sport on television 38 weekends a year.

High-Level Success and Positive Role Models

When elite British athletes succeed on the world stage, participation tends to follow. Swimming participation in the UK rose noticeably after the 2012 Olympics — the “Ellie Simmonds effect” was cited by disability sport organisations as a factor in junior para-swimming club sign-ups. Similarly, Emma Raducanu’s 2021 US Open victory produced a 46% increase in tennis court bookings in the following months. Positive role models make sport feel aspirational and achievable, particularly for young people and for user groups who rarely see someone like them succeeding.

Key Fact

High-level sporting success creates what commentators call the ‘golden generation effect’ — a surge in grassroots participation after elite success. British Cycling’s dominance at the 2012 and 2016 Olympics correlated with a decade-long increase in recreational cycling across all age groups.

Social Acceptability

Social acceptability describes whether a sport is seen as normal, respectable and appropriate for different groups in a given culture. Historically, some sports were considered “not for women” (boxing, rugby) or “too aggressive for respectable families” (martial arts). Cultural shifts, growing media representation, and campaigns like the Rugby Football Union’s “She’s Got Game” initiative have changed these perceptions. Social media has accelerated this: when a sport looks fun and accessible online, social acceptability rises rapidly, particularly among teenagers.

Emerging Sports: What Are They?

An emerging sport is one that is new or rapidly growing in the UK and has not yet achieved mainstream status. Emerging sports typically have a small but enthusiastic participant base, limited facility provision, and are working to establish a national governing body. They often begin as recreational activities before formalising rules and competition structures. The pathway from emerging sport to established sport can take decades — or it can happen very quickly when social media amplifies the sport’s appeal.

Padel: Fast-Growing on UK Courts

Padel is a racket sport played in pairs on an enclosed glass-walled court about a third of the size of a tennis court. It originated in Mexico in the 1960s and became enormous in Spain and Latin America before spreading to the UK. Padel is easier to learn than tennis — the walls mean the ball stays in play longer, so beginners enjoy longer rallies — and it is intensely social. The UK had fewer than 100 padel courts in 2021; by 2025 that number had exceeded 1,000. Padel England secured recognition as the national governing body and affiliated to the Lawn Tennis Association for development support.

Pickleball combines elements of tennis, badminton and table tennis on a smaller court, played with a perforated plastic ball and solid paddles. It is particularly popular with retired people and older adults because the court is smaller, the pace is lower than tennis, and rallies are longer. In 2024, Sport England formally recognised Pickleball England as the sport’s national governing body — a key step in gaining access to lottery funding and local authority facility time. The number of registered pickleball players in England nearly doubled year-on-year between 2023 and 2025.

The factors driving pickleball’s emergence in the UK mirror those for any new sport: low initial cost (courts can be temporarily marked on any hard surface), easy-to-learn rules, high social enjoyment, and growing media coverage on YouTube and social platforms rather than traditional TV.

Not every new sport gains traction. Sports that require expensive specialist equipment, cannot be played in existing facilities, or have rules that are difficult to explain quickly often fail to grow beyond a niche. The absence of a governing body also limits growth — without official recognition, a sport cannot access lottery funding, government facility time, or schools programmes. Social media interest that does not convert to regular, in-person participation also fades quickly. The difference between an emerging sport and a short-lived trend often comes down to whether a committed volunteer community forms clubs, runs competitions, and lobbies for facility access.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For questions about popularity factors, name the specific factor (e.g. ‘media coverage’) and then explain how it increases or decreases participation — not just that it ‘makes sport more popular’. For emerging sports questions, use current named examples: padel and pickleball are both recognised by Sport England. Avoid older examples like ‘snowboarding’ which is now well established, not emerging. If you are asked to ‘discuss’ an emerging sport, consider both why it is growing and what challenges it still faces.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Eight factors drive sport popularity: participation numbers, facilities, climate, live spectator opportunities, media coverage, high-level success, positive role models, and social acceptability — learn all eight with one example each.
  • Padel and pickleball are the UK’s leading emerging sports in 2024–25, both gaining national governing body recognition and growing rapidly in club numbers.
  • Emerging sports need a national governing body, facility access, easy rules and a social media presence to move from trend to established sport.

lessons.title: Values in Sport — Team Spirit, Fair Play & National Pride
lessons.description: How fair play, team spirit, citizenship, national pride and excellence shape sport.
lessons.content_html:
Why Values Matter in Sport

Sport can teach people far more than a skill or a technique. At its best, sport builds character: it demands that we co-operate with teammates, accept decisions from officials, respect opponents, and push ourselves beyond our comfort zone. These qualities are not accidental — they are sporting values: the principles that sport promotes and that participants are expected to show. The specification identifies seven distinct values. Learning them by name and being able to apply each to a specific sporting context is a core exam skill.

Key Fact

The seven sporting values are: team spirit, fair play, citizenship, tolerance and respect (counted as one value in the specification), inclusion, national pride, and excellence. Learn all seven — examiners will penalise answers that miss one or conflate them.

Team Spirit

Team spirit is the collective sense of belonging and mutual support that develops when a group of athletes work toward a shared goal. It is visible when a rugby player sets the ball back for a teammate rather than taking the credit themselves, or when a swimming relay team celebrates every individual's split time as equally important. Team spirit is not just about winning together — it is about maintaining morale during defeat, supporting injured players, and trusting the collective even when individual form is poor. Research consistently shows that teams with strong team spirit outperform their expected ability level in high-pressure situations.

Fair Play

Fair play means playing within both the written rules and the unwritten spirit of a sport. It includes acknowledging good play by an opponent, accepting a referee’s decision without argument, and not seeking an unfair advantage through cheating, gamesmanship or simulation. In football, kicking the ball out of play voluntarily when an opponent is injured — and then returning it when play restarts — is a well-known example of fair play that is not written in the laws of the game but is universally expected. Governing bodies such as The FA and the International Olympic Committee run specific fair play awards to recognise and publicise examples of this value.

Citizenship in sport describes how athletes, clubs and governing bodies contribute positively to the wider community. It goes beyond sport itself: a professional footballer visiting a children’s hospital, a local rugby club providing free sessions to young people at risk of exclusion, or athletes campaigning for environmental sustainability at major events are all examples. Citizenship recognises that elite athletes have a platform and a responsibility to use it for social good.

In school sport, citizenship shows when a team captain encourages a younger student to try the sport, or when athletes volunteer to help at a community event. The value is not just for elite sport — it applies at every level from grassroots to international.

Tolerance and Respect

The specification treats tolerance and respect as a single value. Tolerance means accepting that other people have different backgrounds, beliefs, abilities and approaches to sport. Respect means actively valuing others — opponents, officials, spectators and teammates — regardless of those differences. In practice, this looks like: applauding an opponent’s excellent performance, not arguing with a referee’s call, welcoming athletes from different cultural backgrounds without prejudice, and adapting language and behaviour to make everyone feel included. The Premier League’s “No Room For Racism” campaign is one example of how professional sport institutionalises this value.

Key Fact

Tolerance and respect are listed as a single value — not two separate ones. Older textbooks sometimes split them. The specification wording is ‘tolerance and respect’ as a paired phrase. Always write them together.

Inclusion

Inclusion means ensuring that sport is accessible and welcoming to everyone, regardless of age, gender, disability, ethnicity or socio-economic background. It overlaps with removing barriers but is a value rather than a policy: it describes the attitude sports organisations and participants should hold. Disability sport is one of the clearest expressions of inclusion — the Paralympic movement insists that people with disabilities should have equal opportunities to compete at the highest level, not just take part in modified recreational activities. Inclusion also means mixed-ability sessions, disability-friendly coaching qualifications, and communication in accessible formats.

National Pride

Sport creates one of the most powerful settings for national pride: representing your country at international level, hearing your national anthem before a match, or seeing your flag raised on a medal podium. National pride brings communities together across social divides — for a few weeks during a major tournament, people who would otherwise have little in common find shared identity through their national team. The 2024 Paris Olympics generated significant national pride across the UK, with athletes from diverse backgrounds becoming symbols of national achievement. Research suggests that hosting or succeeding in major sporting events increases public wellbeing beyond the sporting community itself.

Excellence

Excellence in sport is the pursuit of being the very best you can be — not necessarily winning, but striving consistently to improve performance, training habits and competitive standards. The Olympic motto “Citius, Altius, Fortius — Communiter” (Faster, Higher, Stronger — Together) captures this value: the aspiration to continually reach beyond current limits. Excellence is visible in an athlete who trains at 6 am daily, in a club that invests in professional coaching, and in a young performer who asks for feedback and works on their weaknesses rather than coasting on natural ability.

The most common mistake in values questions is vague or circular answers. Writing “fair play means playing fairly” earns no marks. You must name the value, define it precisely, and then anchor it to a specific sporting example. For example: “Fair play is playing within both the rules and the spirit of the sport. An example is a tennis player who calls a ball ‘out’ on their own side, overruling their advantage, because they saw it land in.” The examiner wants definition + applied example. Write both, every time.

Also remember that ‘evaluate’ questions about values ask you to weigh how far sport actually promotes the value — not just to describe what the value is. Real sport also contains examples of values being violated (doping, racism, simulation). A strong evaluative answer acknowledges both sides.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For ‘evaluate’ questions about sporting values, you must argue both sides — examples where sport promotes the value AND examples where the value is violated. A one-sided answer that only shows sport at its best will not reach the top mark band. Always include a specific sporting example to support each point, and end with a justified judgement stating how far you agree overall. Vague statements like ‘sport teaches people to respect each other’ without an example will not score highly — examiners reward applied answers.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The seven sporting values are team spirit, fair play, citizenship, tolerance and respect (one value), inclusion, national pride, and excellence — learn all seven with one example each.
  • Tolerance and respect are treated as a single paired value in the specification — do not split them into two separate values.
  • For evaluation questions, sport can both promote and violate values — you need examples of both sides plus a final judgement to reach the highest mark band.

lessons.title: The Olympic & Paralympic Movement
lessons.description: The Olympic Creed, the five-ring symbol, three Olympic values, and four Paralympic values.
lessons.content_html:
The Olympic and Paralympic Movement

The Olympic and Paralympic Games are the largest peacetime gatherings on the planet — and behind the competition, medals and ceremonies lies a philosophy that has guided international sport for over a century. Understanding the Olympic movement means knowing its founding texts, its symbol and its values — because these are directly assessed and must be recalled precisely.

Pierre de Coubertin and the Olympic Creed

The modern Olympic Games were revived in 1896 by the French educationalist Baron Pierre de Coubertin. He believed that sport could foster international understanding and peace. The philosophy he articulated is preserved in the Olympic Creed:

Key Fact

“The most important thing in the Olympic Games is not to win but to take part, just as the most important thing in life is not the triumph but the struggle. The essential thing is not to have conquered but to have fought well.” — This creed is attributed to Bishop Ethelbert Talbot (1908) and was later adopted by Pierre de Coubertin as the guiding philosophy of the Games.

The Creed emphasises participation over victory, effort over outcome, and the character built through competition over the result itself. It is particularly relevant to athletes who finish outside the medal positions but who have competed to the best of their ability — a quality the Games celebrates through ceremonies such as the Best of the Games awards at Paris 2024.

The Olympic Symbol: Five Interlocking Rings

The Olympic symbol consists of five interlocking rings in blue, yellow, black, green and red on a white background. Designed by Pierre de Coubertin and first used in 1913, the rings represent the five continents of the world — Africa, the Americas, Asia, Europe and Oceania — whose athletes come together at the Games. The interlocking design expresses unity and the crossing of borders through sport.

A common misconception is that each ring represents a specific continent or that the ring colours match specific regions. In fact, the five colours (plus white) were chosen because every nation’s flag contains at least one of these six colours — the rings do not individually represent specific continents. The symbol is the most recognised sporting logo in the world and is a protected trademark of the International Olympic Committee.

The Olympic movement is built on three core values. The first is Excellence — the pursuit of being the best in body, mind and spirit; striving to perform at the highest level and to give of one’s best in whatever one undertakes. At Paris 2024, Dina Asher-Smith preparing for the 100m final — studying rivals, honing technique, choosing the right mental warm-up — embodied this value before she even reached the start line.

The second is Respect — respect for oneself, for other athletes, for the rules, for the environment and for the spectators. It is shown in post-race handshakes, in athletes challenging unfair calls through proper channels rather than confrontation, and in competitors carrying an injured rival across the finish line (as happened memorably at a 2019 World University Games race).

The third is Friendship — using sport to build bridges between people of different backgrounds, nationalities and beliefs. The Olympic Village at Paris 2024 housed over 14,500 athletes from 206 nations in one location, creating connections across borders that no diplomatic summit could replicate. Friendship is also seen in dual-nationality partnerships, mixed-relay events that pair athletes from different countries, and the tradition of trading national badges and pins.

Key Fact

Olympic values (three): Excellence, Respect, Friendship. Paralympic values (four): Courage, Determination, Inspiration, Equality. These are closed lists — they must be reproduced exactly. Students who mix them up or paraphrase them lose marks.

The Four Paralympic Values

The Paralympic movement has its own set of four values that reflect the distinctive experience of athletes with a disability competing at the highest level. The first is Courage — the bravery to compete, to push physical limits, and to confront any stigma around disability in public life. The second is Determination — the relentless effort needed to reach elite level, often against greater obstacles than non-disabled athletes face in access to coaching, funding and facilities.

The third is Inspiration — the power of Paralympic athletes to change attitudes toward disability in society, encouraging people with disabilities to participate and encouraging non-disabled people to reconsider assumptions about what the human body can do. At Paris 2024, British blind triathlete Dave Ellis and guide Luke Pollard’s gold medal was widely cited by UK disability charities as inspiring a wave of enquiries to para-triathlon clubs. The fourth is Equality — the belief that all people, regardless of disability, deserve equal opportunities to participate and compete in sport at every level.

Olympic and Paralympic values are not just abstract principles — they are embedded in specific campaigns and initiatives at local, regional and national level. At local level: a community sports club that runs a ‘have-a-go’ session for young people with disabilities is putting Equality and Inspiration into practice. At regional level: a county sports partnership that brings together athletes from rival clubs for a joint values day puts Friendship and Respect at the centre. At national level: UK Sport’s “Inspiring a Generation” legacy programme from 2012 continued to fund grassroots sport for a decade, directly linking Olympic success to community participation.

Schools can also embed these values through curriculum sport: competitive house events that reward Determination as much as results, or team challenges that deliberately mix year groups to build Friendship. The specification asks students to recognise examples at all three levels — so think local, regional and national when answering.

Students frequently swap the two sets of values. A common error is writing “Courage” as an Olympic value (it is Paralympic) or writing “Friendship” as a Paralympic value (it is Olympic). The simplest memory aid: Olympic values have three items (Excellence, Respect, Friendship); Paralympic values have four items (Courage, Determination, Inspiration, Equality). If you are asked for both sets in one question, list them separately with the correct heading.
lessons.exam_tip_html: If a question asks you to ‘identify’ an Olympic or Paralympic value, write it exactly as it appears: ‘Excellence’, ‘Respect’, ‘Friendship’ for Olympic; ‘Courage’, ‘Determination’, ‘Inspiration’, ‘Equality’ for Paralympic. If asked to ‘explain’ a value, define it and then give a specific sporting example — a general statement like ‘it means being brave’ without an example will score only 1 of 3 marks. Do not mix Olympic and Paralympic values in the same list. For the Olympic Creed, you do not need to quote it word-for-word in an exam, but you must show you understand its central message: participation and effort matter more than winning.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Olympic Creed states that the most important thing is ‘not to win but to take part’; it was adopted by Pierre de Coubertin and expresses that effort and participation matter more than victory.
  • The five interlocking rings represent the five continents whose athletes meet at the Games; the five colours plus white appear in every national flag in the world.
  • Olympic values (three): Excellence, Respect, Friendship. Paralympic values (four): Courage, Determination, Inspiration, Equality. Learn them separately — mixing them up loses marks.

practice_questions.text:
Oakfield Academy runs a sports day for Year 9 students. The head of PE wants to redesign the event so that it promotes Olympic and Paralympic values, not just competitive winning. The event currently awards medals only for finishing first, second and third.

Discuss how Oakfield Academy could redesign its sports day to promote Olympic and Paralympic values across the whole event.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): A developed discussion covering at least two values from each movement with specific redesign proposals. For example: add a sportsmanship award to embed Respect; introduce team relay events where all ability levels are mixed to promote Friendship; include events specifically for students with disabilities to promote Equality and Courage; reward consistent effort over the year to embody Excellence and Determination. The answer considers both what to add and potential challenges (cost, time, student buy-in), and presents more than one viewpoint.
Secure (3–4 marks): Two or more values named with some linked suggestions, but coverage may be thin.
Developing (2 marks): One value mentioned with one suggestion, or two values without proposals.
Emerging (1 mark): A single relevant point. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Clayfield Sports College has been invited to host an Olympic Values Day for local primary schools. The college must design activities that bring the Olympic Creed and at least two Olympic values to life for pupils aged 9 and 10.

Evaluate how effectively an Olympic Values Day could promote the Olympic Creed and the values of Excellence and Friendship among primary school pupils, considering both what could be achieved and the challenges involved.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8 marks): A balanced evaluation that identifies how the Creed and both values could be promoted (e.g. design activities where participation and effort are rewarded over results, linking directly to 'not to win but to take part'; mixed-school team challenges that require co-operation across strangers to build Friendship; achievement ladders rather than league tables for Excellence). The answer then challenges these by arguing that competitive children and teachers accustomed to results-based sport may resist non-competitive framing; that a single day is insufficient to embed values; that without follow-up in PE lessons the impact fades. A clear, substantiated judgement concludes how effective such a day could be — acknowledging that it creates awareness but that sustainable promotion requires curriculum embedding. No judgement = cannot reach Mastering.
Secure (5–6 marks): Two or more arguments on each side with some development; judgement present.
Developing (3–4 marks): Relevant points but one-sided or no judgement.
Emerging (1–2 marks): Basic description of the Creed or values with no evaluation. [8 marks]

lessons.title: Etiquette, Sportsmanship & Spectator Behaviour
lessons.description: Sportsmanship vs gamesmanship, etiquette in action, and how spectators can help or harm sport.
lessons.content_html:
What Is Etiquette in Sport?

Etiquette refers to the expected standards of behaviour in sport that go beyond the written rules. While rules tell players what they must do, etiquette tells them what they should do to show respect for the sport, opponents, officials and spectators. Etiquette varies between sports but always promotes fair and respectful participation.

Common examples of etiquette include shaking hands with opponents after a match, applauding good play by the opposition, walking off the pitch when injured without making a fuss, and accepting the referee’s decision without argument. In tennis, players wait for a break in play before retrieving an errant ball rather than disrupting a point. In cricket, a fielder tells the umpire honestly if they grounded a catch.

Key Fact

Etiquette is the unwritten code of conduct in sport. It includes acts like shaking hands after a game, applauding the opposition, and kicking the ball out of play when an opponent is injured — all gestures that show respect without being required by the rules.

Sportsmanship vs Gamesmanship

Sportsmanship means playing within the written rules AND the spirit of the sport. A player demonstrating sportsmanship competes hard but never at the expense of fairness or respect. Sporting behaviour includes playing to win within the rules, showing respect to the referee even when you disagree, and putting the welfare of an injured opponent above the advantage of the game.

Gamesmanship, by contrast, involves bending the spirit of the rules to gain a competitive edge — without breaking them outright. A football player taking a long time over a throw-in to waste a few seconds is using gamesmanship. So is a tennis player taking unusually long between serves to disrupt an opponent’s rhythm, or a cricketer deliberately moving in a fielder’s line of sight just before a delivery.

Many students confuse these two terms. Remember: sportsmanship is doing the right thing even when the rules do not force you to. Gamesmanship is doing something that is technically legal but goes against the spirit of the sport. A handy paired example to remember: kicking the ball out of play for an injured opponent (sportsmanship) versus slowing down a throw-in to waste time (gamesmanship). The question will often ask for “one applied example of each” — always give a specific sporting situation, not a vague description.

Values That Underpin Sporting Behaviour

Sporting behaviour is underpinned by shared values that sport is meant to promote. Fair play is the idea that competition should be decided by ability and effort, not by cheating. Respect means treating opponents, officials and teammates with dignity. Tolerance means accepting differences — in skill level, background or playing style — without hostility. These values explain why etiquette and sportsmanship matter beyond any single match: they preserve sport as a positive experience for everyone involved.

Key Fact

Sportsmanship requires playing within both the letter of the rules (what is written) and the spirit of the rules (what the sport is meant to stand for). Gamesmanship only respects the letter — it exploits gaps in the rules for personal gain.

Spectator Behaviour

Spectators play a major role in the atmosphere of any sporting event. Positive spectator behaviour includes cheering your team, applauding great play from either side, staying within designated areas, and following ground regulations. These behaviours create an enjoyable and safe environment for everyone — athletes, officials and fellow spectators.

Negative spectator behaviour, however, can have serious consequences. Hooliganism refers to disorderly or violent behaviour by fans. This can include fighting in and around stadiums, chanting abuse, throwing objects onto the pitch, or invading the playing surface. Hooliganism puts players, officials and other fans at risk. It can also lead to matches being abandoned, grounds being closed and the sport’s reputation being damaged.

Following the Hillsborough disaster in April 1989 — a crowd crush at Sheffield Wednesday’s ground that ultimately claimed 97 Liverpool supporters (95 died at the scene, a 96th in 1993, and a 97th in 2021; the campaign was historically known as Justice for the 96) — Lord Justice Taylor produced the Taylor Report (1990). Its central recommendation was that top-flight football grounds in England should become all-seater stadia, replacing terraces where standing spectators could become dangerously compressed. By 1994–95, all Premier League and First Division grounds had converted. All-seater stadia give every fan an assigned seat, reduce crowd surges, and allow stewards to monitor and remove individuals causing problems more easily. They are now considered an essential safety standard in modern football.

The shift to all-seater grounds also changed the culture of watching football. Individual ticketing reduced the anonymity that could mask troublemakers, and CCTV coverage became far easier to implement. Crowd segregation — separating home and away supporters — was formalised. Together, these measures contributed to a significant fall in football-related disorder from the 1990s onwards.

Spectators’ Responsibilities

Spectators are not passive bystanders. They have responsibilities to the performers, to officials, and to each other. Accepting referee decisions without confronting officials, avoiding language or actions that intimidate players, and not engaging in discriminatory chanting are all expectations placed on spectators. Ground regulations typically prohibit entering the field of play, and spectators can be ejected or banned for breaking these rules.

Some stadiums use “ultras” — highly organised and passionate fan groups, typically associated with European football. While many ultras create spectacular displays using flags, banners and coordinated chanting, the culture has at times been linked to disorder. The key distinction for the exam is between passionate support (acceptable) and threatening or violent behaviour (unacceptable and illegal).

Poor spectator behaviour has direct consequences: events can be cancelled or moved, clubs can be fined or have grounds closed, international reputations suffer, and broadcasters can lose confidence in covering the sport. On the other hand, a vocal and well-behaved crowd enhances the experience for everyone, creates a positive atmosphere and encourages participation. Examiners often ask students to explain how spectator behaviour can affect the sport as a whole — think about impact on the game, the club, the players and the wider image of sport.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Questions on this topic often use command words like “describe” or “explain.” When asked to describe an example of sportsmanship or gamesmanship, always name a specific sporting situation — not just “a player was respectful.” For a ‘6 marks — Discuss’ question on spectator behaviour, you must cover more than one point of view: consider the impact on players, officials, other spectators and the sport’s reputation. A common mistake is writing only about safety risks and forgetting the reputational and financial consequences of poor spectator behaviour. Always finish a discuss answer by linking points together, not just listing them.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Etiquette is the unwritten code of conduct in sport — acts like shaking hands and applauding opponents show respect beyond what the rules require.
  • Sportsmanship means honouring both the letter and the spirit of the sport; gamesmanship exploits loopholes without breaking rules. They are not the same thing.
  • Spectators have responsibilities too — hooliganism damages sport’s image and safety. The Taylor Report (1990) led to all-seater stadia in English football as a direct response to crowd disasters.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is an example of sportsmanship?
A) A basketball player deliberately elbowing an opponent when the referee is not looking
B) A footballer kicking the ball out of play so an injured opponent can receive treatment
C) A tennis player bouncing the ball unusually slowly to unsettle a nervous opponent before serving
D) A rugby player disputing every decision made by the referee throughout the match
practice_questions.marks: B) A footballer kicking the ball out of play so an injured opponent can receive treatment [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two examples of negative spectator behaviour at a live sporting event.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark for each genuinely distinct example (maximum 2 marks). Acceptable answers include:
- Throwing objects onto the pitch / at players or officials
- Pitch invasion / entering the field of play without permission
- Racist or abusive chanting directed at players
- Fighting between rival supporters
- Using pyrotechnics (flares, smoke bombs) in the crowd
- Verbally intimidating officials or players
Do not award a second mark if both answers are essentially the same point (e.g. 'shouting abuse' and 'chanting abuse').

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between sportsmanship and gamesmanship. Give one example of each.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark for a clear definition of sportsmanship (playing within the letter and spirit of the rules / showing respect for the sport and opponents). Award 1 mark for a clear definition or description of gamesmanship (bending the rules / exploiting loopholes without technically breaking them). Award 1 mark for a relevant, applied example of each:
- Sportsmanship example: e.g. kicking the ball out for an injured player; shaking hands after a defeat; accepting a referee's call without complaint
- Gamesmanship example: e.g. time-wasting at a throw-in; bouncing the ball slowly before a serve; calling an injury to disrupt opposition momentum
All 3 marks can be awarded without mentioning both examples if the definitions are sufficiently precise and applied.

practice_questions.text: Describe two ways in which poor spectator behaviour can negatively affect a sporting event. Give one example from sport to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks. Credit two distinct negative effects (up to 2 marks each) with development:
- Safety risks: fans may be injured or killed (e.g. crowd crushes, fighting). Reference to Hillsborough 1989 or similar crowd disaster is creditworthy.
- Match disruption / abandonment: incidents of pitch invasion, flares or serious fighting may force officials to stop play.
- Reputational damage: the sport or club is associated with disorder, deterring families, sponsors and broadcasters.
- Financial penalty: governing bodies can fine clubs, close grounds or impose points deductions following crowd trouble.
A named sporting example is required for the top marks on the second point. A generic answer with no named example is capped at 2 marks.

practice_questions.text:
Kingsmere FC is a non-league football club in Worcestershire. After a closely contested local derby, a group of away supporters entered the pitch and confronted home players. The club received a warning from the county FA.

Discuss how spectator behaviour, both positive and negative, can affect a football club like Kingsmere FC.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): Balanced discussion covering both positive and negative spectator behaviour, with development of at least two distinct effects in each direction. Points are linked and interact (e.g. one negative consequence leads to another). Named or applied examples used. Judgement or synthesis attempted.

Secure (3-4 marks): At least two effects discussed, one positive and one negative, with some development beyond a simple list. Limited interaction between points.

Developing (2 marks): Two or more valid effects stated but with little development. May be one-sided (only positives or only negatives).

Emerging (1 mark): A single valid point about spectator behaviour with no development.

Credit points such as: positive atmosphere lifts player performance; community identity and belonging; negative behaviour leads to fines, ground closures, point deductions; physical safety risks; reputational damage to club and sport; impact on sponsorship and media coverage.

practice_questions.text: Give two examples of etiquette that might be observed in any sport of your choice.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark per distinct and relevant etiquette example (maximum 2 marks). Answers must name or clearly describe a specific expected behaviour rather than a vague statement. Acceptable examples:
- Shaking hands with opponents / officials after a match
- Applauding good play by the opposing team or player
- Acknowledging when a ball was out that was called in (e.g. tennis)
- Kicking the ball out for an injured opponent in football
- Walking off the field promptly when given out in cricket
- Waiting for a break in play before collecting a stray ball (tennis / badminton)
Do not award if both examples are essentially the same behaviour described differently.

lessons.title: Performance-Enhancing Drugs, WADA & Sanctions
lessons.description: Why athletes use PEDs, how WADA and the Whereabouts Rule work, and what sanctions rule-breakers face.
lessons.content_html:
Why Do Athletes Use Performance-Enhancing Drugs?

Performance-enhancing drugs (PEDs) are substances that give athletes a competitive advantage. Reasons why athletes choose to use them include the enormous financial rewards available at the elite level, intense pressure from coaches, sponsors and national expectations, and the belief that “everyone else is doing it.” In some nations there has been state-sponsored doping — the Russian doping programme uncovered before the 2016 Rio Olympics is the clearest modern example. Injuries, quick recovery demands, and the desire to maintain performance as the body ages also push some athletes towards banned substances.

Key Fact

Reasons for using PEDs include financial rewards, competitive pressure, fear of falling behind rivals, and national expectation. Reasons against include health risks, ban from sport, reputational damage, acting as a negative role model, and the unfair advantage over clean competitors.

Why Athletes Should NOT Use PEDs

The case against PED use is equally strong. Many banned substances carry serious health risks: heart problems, hormonal imbalances, liver damage and psychological effects have all been documented. Beyond health, using PEDs violates the principle of fair play — clean athletes are denied a level playing field. Elite athletes are also role models: when they are caught doping, they send a damaging message to young people that cheating is an acceptable path to success. Athletes who test positive face heavy sanctions, public humiliation, and often have their results stripped retrospectively. The sport itself suffers reputational damage that can take decades to repair.

The Role of WADA

The World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) was founded in 1999 and is the international organisation responsible for the fight against doping in sport. WADA publishes the Prohibited List — updated annually — which names every banned substance and method. The list groups substances into ten categories (S0–S9): non-approved substances, anabolic agents, peptide hormones and growth factors, beta-2 agonists, hormone and metabolic modulators, diuretics and masking agents, stimulants, narcotics, cannabinoids, and glucocorticoids. Three further categories (M1–M3) cover prohibited methods (such as blood doping and gene doping). Beta-blockers and alcohol are listed separately as banned only in particular sports — archery and shooting for beta-blockers; archery and motorsport for alcohol. WADA sets the standards; national organisations — such as UKAD (UK Anti-Doping) — enforce those standards within their own country.

Key Fact

WADA was founded in 1999. It publishes the annual Prohibited List covering nine categories of banned substances and methods. In the UK, UKAD enforces the WADA Code on behalf of sport. The Whereabouts Rule is one of WADA’s most important enforcement tools.

The Whereabouts Rule

One of WADA’s most important anti-doping tools is the Whereabouts Rule. Athletes in the “Registered Testing Pool” must file quarterly Whereabouts submissions declaring where they will be — including a specific one-hour window each day (e.g. 7am–8am at home) when testers can arrive unannounced. Out-of-competition testing is considered vital because many PEDs are used during training rather than at competition itself.

If an athlete accumulates three missed tests or filing failures within any 12-month rolling period, this counts as an anti-doping rule violation — the same as actually failing a drug test. Athletes and their agents use the ADAMS (Anti-Doping Administration and Management System) online platform to submit Whereabouts information. The rule is demanding but is seen as essential to catch sophisticated doping programmes that use substances that clear the body quickly.

Students often know that athletes must “tell someone where they are” but cannot explain the specific mechanics that examiners want. Make sure you know three things: (1) it is a one-hour window per day where an athlete must be reachable; (2) athletes submit information quarterly in advance; and (3) three missed tests or filing failures in 12 months triggers a violation. The examiner report identifies this as the most commonly underscored knowledge gap on the doping topic.

Testing Methods

Anti-doping tests are conducted both in-competition (at events) and out-of-competition (during training). Athletes may be called for testing immediately after competing or visited at a training site without warning. Testing uses urine samples and blood samples. Blood passporting — tracking an athlete’s biological markers over time — allows authorities to detect patterns of doping even when a specific substance cannot be found in a single test. High-profile cases such as the Russian Athletics Investigation Federation (Russian athletes competed as “AIN” at Paris 2024 due to ongoing sanctions) demonstrate how systematic doping can be identified and punished at a national level.

Sanctions for Doping

Sanctions escalate depending on the substance involved, whether it was intentional, and whether the athlete has offended before. The typical sanctions ladder runs: formal warnings for minor first-time administrative breaches → fines → competition bans (ranging from one year to a lifetime ban) → criminal prosecution for those found trafficking banned substances. Results achieved during a doping period are typically annulled, meaning medals, records and prize money are returned.

High-profile cases illustrate the consequences: swimmer Sun Yang received an eight-year ban (later revised on appeal) for refusing to cooperate with anti-doping testers. Russia’s track and field athletes were barred from competing under the Russian flag at the Tokyo 2020 and Paris 2024 Olympics as a direct result of a state-sponsored doping programme. These cases reinforce that the consequences of doping extend beyond the individual to national sporting programmes.

Testing alone is not enough — education strategies are equally important. UKAD runs “100% Me” as an anti-doping education programme for young athletes, emphasising clean sport values and the risks of supplements. Schools and sports clubs are encouraged to discuss the ethics of doping openly. Role models who compete cleanly and speak out against doping are a powerful deterrent — young athletes are more likely to follow the example of athletes they admire than to respond to a rulebook alone. Nutrition education also helps athletes understand which legal supplements carry contamination risks that could produce a positive test.
lessons.exam_tip_html: The 8-mark Evaluate question on this topic might ask: “Should performance-enhancing drugs be legalised in elite sport?” To reach the top band you need a balanced argument (reasons for legalising AND reasons against), at least one applied example (e.g. Russia’s AIN status at Paris 2024, the Whereabouts Rule, UKAD enforcement), and a justified conclusion — your final judgement must be supported by the strongest point you’ve made. A common failure is writing only one side (usually “drugs are bad”) and not attempting to argue the counter-position fairly. Even if you disagree with legalisation, you must present its strongest case and then refute it clearly. Remember: no board names or codes in your answer — just the issue and the evidence.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Athletes use PEDs for financial rewards, competitive pressure and national expectation — but health risks, sanctions, reputational damage and negative role-modelling are strong reasons not to.
  • WADA (founded 1999) publishes the annual Prohibited List. UKAD enforces it in the UK. The Whereabouts Rule requires a daily one-hour location window; three missed tests in 12 months equals a violation.
  • Sanctions escalate from warnings and fines to multi-year bans, result annulment and criminal prosecution for trafficking. Education strategies and role models complement testing as deterrents.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes the role of WADA?
A) A UK-only body that tests athletes for banned substances at major competitions
B) An international organisation that sets the global Prohibited List and co-ordinates anti-doping testing across sport
C) A government department that decides on prison sentences for athletes caught doping
D) A sports court that hears appeals from athletes who fail drug tests
practice_questions.marks: B) An international organisation that sets the global Prohibited List and co-ordinates anti-doping testing across sport [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two reasons why an elite athlete might choose to use a performance-enhancing drug.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark per distinct reason (maximum 2 marks). Acceptable answers include:
- Financial rewards / prize money available at elite level
- Competitive pressure (from coaches, sponsors, nation)
- Belief that rivals are already using PEDs
- Pressure to recover quickly from injury
- State-sponsored / institutional doping culture
- Desire to extend career as the body ages
Do not award a second mark for answers that are essentially the same point rephrased.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the Whereabouts Rule helps to deter doping in elite sport.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks:
- 1 mark: state what the Whereabouts Rule is (athletes must declare their location for one hour each day for unannounced testing)
- 1 mark: explain why this deters doping (testers can arrive without warning; athletes cannot time their drug use to avoid tests)
- 1 mark: apply or develop the point (e.g. three missed tests in 12 months equals a violation; out-of-competition testing catches substances used during training that clear the body by race day; athletes submit information quarterly via ADAMS)

practice_questions.text: Describe the sanctions an athlete might face if they tested positive for a banned substance. Use an example from sport to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks. Credit must cover the sanctions ladder AND include at least one named example:
- Warning / formal caution (minor or first-time breach)
- Fine
- Competition ban (length varies: 1 year to lifetime; 4-year ban standard for first serious offence under 2021 Code)
- Results annulment (medals, records, prize money returned)
- Criminal prosecution for trafficking
Named example (required for top marks): Sun Yang (extended ban for refusing cooperation with testers); Russian athletes competing as AIN at Paris 2024 following state-sponsored doping programme; any other accurately described real case. An answer with no named sporting example is capped at 2 marks.

practice_questions.text:
Riverside Harriers is an athletics club in Yorkshire. Their star 800m runner, Connor, is in the national Registered Testing Pool. Last year, testers visited three times when he was not at his declared location. He says he simply forgot to update his details.

Discuss whether education strategies alone are enough to prevent doping in sport, using the scenario above to help frame your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): Balanced discussion that addresses at least two arguments in favour of education being sufficient AND at least one argument that testing/sanctions are also needed. Points interact: e.g. education raises awareness but determined cheaters require enforcement. The scenario is referenced or applied meaningfully. Development beyond a list.

Secure (3-4 marks): At least two valid points on different sides, with some development. Scenario may be referenced but not fully applied.

Developing (2 marks): Two or more valid points stated with limited development, likely one-sided.

Emerging (1 mark): A single valid point about education or anti-doping with no development.

Credit: education raises awareness early; role models are powerful; supplements education reduces inadvertent positives. BUT: financial incentives remain; determined cheaters will not be deterred by values alone; Whereabouts / testing catches those education misses; sanctions provide a real deterrent. The scenario shows that even administrative failings (not knowing/following the Whereabouts Rule) require enforcement not just education.

practice_questions.text:
'Performance-enhancing drugs should be legalised in elite sport so that athletes can compete on an equal footing.'

Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): Sophisticated, balanced evaluation. Arguments for legalisation are presented fairly and fully (e.g. would create a level playing field if all could access the same substances; reduces hypocrisy of selective testing; athletes as consenting adults; difficult/expensive to police). Arguments against are equally developed (health risks, especially long-term; sets a damaging example for young and junior athletes; undermines the value of natural talent and training; access inequalities — wealthier athletes/nations could afford better drugs; erosion of sport's values). A clear, justified conclusion is reached, not just stated. Applied sporting example used (e.g. Russian state-doping scandal; Prohibited List enforcement).

Secure (5-6 marks): Clear argument on both sides with relevant evidence. A conclusion is present but may not be fully substantiated. Some applied context.

Developing (3-4 marks): Some argument on both sides. Evidence is limited or assertion-based. Conclusion may be missing or undeveloped.
